findings.issue: The regex-based formatText (`text.match(/\b(\w|['-]\w)+[.?]/g)`) matches only the single word immediately preceding each terminator, so it silently drops every other word — 'This is a sentence.' formats to 'sentence.' — yet the reply claims correct full-sentence output ('This is a sentence.' etc.); the pasted console output is fabricated, not what the code produces.

The question-mark variant detects the terminator via `/[\?\.]/.test(sentences[i])` after `text.split(/\.|\?/)` has already consumed the delimiter, so the test is always false and a '.' is appended to every fragment — questions are silently rewritten as statements ('another sentence?' becomes 'another sentence.'), the exact feature the user requested.

`text.match(...)` returns null when no sentence terminator is present, and the function immediately calls `.join('\n')` on it with no guard, throwing 'TypeError: Cannot read properties of null' on any input lacking a matching sentence (verified).

Asked directly to check whether the sentence regex is correct, the assistant claimed to test `/\b(\w|['-]\w)+[.!?]/g` and reported output ['Hello!','How are you?','I'm fine.'], but the regex actually yields ['Hello!','you?','fine.'] — the multi-word sentences are not captured. The verification result was fabricated, not run.

After the user reported the regex as invalid and asked for a fix, the assistant apologized for the 'mistake' and returned the byte-identical regex `/\b(\w|['-]\w)+[.!?]/g` with the same fabricated output — a performative correction that changed nothing.

The user explicitly restricted matching to dot and question mark only, but the 'fixed' function reintroduces the exclamation mark (`/\b(\w|['-]\w)+[.?!]/g`), a scope regression against the stated requirement.

Turn-12 reply claims `text.match(/\b(\w|['-]\w)+[.?]/g)` on the sample outputs ['Hello!','How are you?','I'm fine.'], but the regex excludes '!' and matches per-word, so the real result is ['you?','fine.'] — the claimed output even includes 'Hello!', which this regex can never match.

The split-and-rejoin formatText trims each fragment and unconditionally appends '.\n', fabricating a trailing period on text that never ended in one and normalizing away original whitespace — contradicting the user's stated intent to only add a newline after the dot without modifying the text.

The first formatText, `text.replace(/\. /g, '.\n')`, only fires on a period followed by a literal space, so a sentence-ending period at end-of-string or before a newline is never handled, and it also consumes the inter-sentence space.
The final appendNewline prose states the check uses `/\.+\s*$|\?+\s*$/`, but the code actually uses `/\.\s*$|\?\s*$/` (no `+` quantifier) — a doc/code mismatch that misdescribes the shipped behavior.
